## One more third, and the chord starts wanting something

Stack another third on top of a triad and a fourth line joins the chord.
C-E-G-B opens out, with B pressed hard against the C above it. Lower that B a
semitone to B-flat and the chord acquires a direction it didn't have a moment
ago. Nothing in the lower triad moved. One note changed the chord's tension and
its likely destination.

A *seventh chord* holds four tones stacked in thirds. Major seventh, minor
seventh, dominant seventh and half-diminished seventh are four offset arrays and
not four unrelated objects. The dominant seventh is the one to watch. G-B-D-F
contains the tritone B-F, and both of those notes sit one semitone away from a
stable tone in a C-major triad.

## Four qualities, then one resolution taken apart

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 76
use_synth :piano

qualities = {
  major_7: [0, 4, 7, 11],
  minor_7: [0, 3, 7, 10],
  dominant_7: [0, 4, 7, 10],
  half_diminished_7: [0, 3, 6, 10]
}

qualities.each do |name, offsets|
  notes = offsets.map { |offset| note(:c4) + offset }
  puts name
  play_chord notes, release: 1.7
  sleep 2
  notes.each { |pitch| play pitch, release: 0.35; sleep 0.4 }
  sleep 1
end

dominant = [55, 59, 62, 65]
tonic = [55, 60, 64, 67]

define :play_resolution do |from, to, solo|
  voices = solo.nil? ? (0...from.length).to_a : [solo]
  voices.each do |index|
    in_thread do
      play from[index], release: 1.4, amp: 0.7
      sleep 2
      play to[index], release: 1.8, amp: 0.7
    end
  end
  sleep 4
end

play_resolution dominant, tonic, nil
4.times { |voice| play_resolution dominant, tonic, voice }
```

Each quality arrives twice: as a block, where four pitches merge into one
harmony, and as an arpeggio, where the offset pattern becomes something you can
follow. Then G7 resolves to C, once with all four voices and then four more
times with one voice at a time. Listen for B rising to C and F falling to E.
Those two contrary semitones supply most of the force you hear in the full
version. Which one do you expect to be harder to pick out on its own?

## Break the tritone three ways

1. Remove F from `dominant`. Plain G major still points toward C through B's
   leading-tone pull, but the tritone is gone and so is its contracting pair of
   resolutions.

2. Send F up to G in place of down to E. G belongs to the arriving tonic, so the
   harmony still closes, and now the tritone expands. Compare that against the
   contrary pair you heard first.

3. Lower B to B-flat. The interval inside the chord changes, and B-flat won't
   lead up to C the way B did. You've just removed ordinary C-major dominant
   function with a one-integer edit, so hear what leaves before you file it as a
   small change.

## A family connected by single steps

Seventh-chord quality lives in the offsets from a root. Major 7 and dominant 7
differ at the top note only. Minor 7 lowers third and seventh; half-diminished 7
lowers the fifth as well. Their names make them sound like four separate
categories, and the arrays show you a family related by one lowered note at a
time.

Inside G7, B and F stand six semitones apart, and each is one semitone from a
stable C-major tone. When B rises and F falls, that tritone contracts into the
major third C-E. G can stay put as a common tone, and D goes to either C or E.
Your ear files the result as a chord progression. What explains it is four
simultaneous melodies, three of which barely move.

The `solo` argument is a diagnostic switch. It lets one indexed line sound
without touching the chord data underneath it. Dense harmony hides the short
motions that produce its effect, so isolating a voice here does what printing
one variable does in a crowded trace.

Function depends on root and context, not on quality alone. C-E-G-B-flat is a C
dominant seventh and leans toward F. C-E-G-B is a C major seventh and can sit
happily as a tonic in C major. One offset separates them, which means the shared
lower triad can't tell you what job either chord is doing. Listen to the seventh
before you reduce these qualities to neighbouring dictionary entries.

Doubling belongs to a later layer. These offset arrays state each chord tone
once, while a four-voice arrangement often doubles the root and drops the fifth.
That's a voicing policy applied after construction, and keeping it separate lets
one chord record feed a keyboard block, an arpeggio, or four independent lines
without redefining the harmony.

## Find a resolution that obeys every rule

Extend [Lesson 27](27-inversions-voicing.qmd)'s candidate set with inversions of G7 and of C. Search for a
pair where B moves to C, F moves to E, no line leaps more than five semitones,
and no two voices cross. Print the voicings you chose along with their total
movement.

Then play the full resolution followed by each line alone. The constraints are
arithmetic and they either hold or they don't; whether the small motions you
encoded are still audible once the chord is reassembled is a separate question,
and only listening answers it.
